title: The popular version. The Bayeux Tapestry is a tapestry.
description:
The Bayeux Tapestry is a tapestry. The scenes are stitched onto linen, not woven into it. That makes it an embroidery.

Roughly its length. Sources give 68.38 metres, made from nine linen panels sewn together.

About ten colours of wool. Worked in wool on linen, with dyes made from plant material.

Probably English hands made it. Most scholars favour Canterbury. It was probably commissioned by Odo, Bishop of Bayeux.

Its first written mention is 1476. A Bayeux Cathedral inventory lists it. That is the earliest known reference.

The name stuck. The technique did not.

Sources:
- https://www.worldhistory.org/Bayeux_Tapestry/: read in full (World History Encyclopedia). Established that it is really an embroidery as the scenes are stitched not woven, 68.38 metres in length, two ply wool yarn dyed from plant material in at least ten colours, 58 scenes, most likely made by embroiderers in Canterbury, probably for Odo, Bishop of Bayeux, and first listed in the cathedral inventory in 1476.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayeux_Tapestry: first 39,946 of 87,200 characters read verbatim. Established technically an embroidery rather than a true tapestry, 68.38 m long, nine linen panels sewn together, wool thread on linen in ten natural dye colours, 58 scenes, probably made in or around Canterbury according to most contemporary scholars, generally thought to be commissioned by Odo, and a 1476 inventory as the earliest known written reference.
- https://www.bayeuxmuseum.com/en/tapestry-or-embroidery/: read in full (Bayeux Museum). Established that the technique is unquestionably embroidery, that a tapestry's design emerges from weaving threads at right angles, nine linen panels joined together, about 68.3 metres long and ten colours of wool thread, and that most historians believe Odo commissioned it.
